Crop test — every photograph in every container

Each file rendered with object-fit: cover at each shape — the browser is doing the crop, not a simulation, so what you see is what ships. Shapes run narrowest to widest, so a photograph degrades left to right. Resize the window and it all re-crops live.

Containers · source is 3:2
ShapeRoleSizeKeepsNote
1:1Avatar / square thumbnail80 · 16067% of widthCrops width hard — keeps 67% of a 3:2 source. Off-centre subjects and side-by-side pairs lose out.
4:3Thumbnail160×12089% of widthCrops width lightly — trims 11%.
3:2Split hero · editorial card600×400100% of widthNative shape. No crop at all — the control.
16:10Wide cardcolumn × 20094% of heightCrops height by 6%. Effectively safe.
16:9Programme tilecolumn × 24084% of heightCrops height — keeps 84%. Loses hats, hair, headroom.
2:1Banner / promo strip1280 × 64075% of heightKeeps 75% of height. The first shape where headroom really goes.
3:1Wide banner1440 × 48050% of heightKeeps 50% of height. Faces start to go.
4:1Full-width hero at desktop1440 × 36038% of heightKeeps 37.5% of height. Where faces get cut.
hero 4.5:1Full-bleed hero + overlay text1440 × 32033% of heightThe overlay-text hero from image-sizing.md (280–320dp tall). Keeps 33%.
6:1Page header1440 × 24025% of heightKeeps 25% of height. Anything failing 4:1 fails here too.
ViewShapes in the row

Fewer shapes in the row means bigger pictures. Add or drop any shape — the row re-flows and the images stay legible.

Fails at least one container62

The crop cuts through the face, or the subject reduces to an unidentifiable body part. Still usable in the shapes it passes — the outline marks the ones it doesn't.
